paper_title: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, with progress driven largely by scaling model size and omni training data. We ask whether a model needs to hear the audio directly at all, and present SleuthVLM, an agent harness built on a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech will be transcribed into text, and the VLM will sleuth the video on its own without any predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, SleuthVLM achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it also tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8%}; with an open-source 27B VLM, it beats all open-source omni models. We draw three findings: SleuthVLM beats a model that glances; hearing is not the bottleneck, agentic ability is; omni understanding needs better agentic ability, not just more omni data for modality alignment. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding. Omni understanding needs better agents, not just bigger models that hear.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Many questions about videos require understanding both visual and audio content. Omni models address this task by combining vision-language model (VLM) with an audio encoder and training on paired omni data, enabling them to answer questions from sampled frames and the audio track in one turn. Closed-source models such as Gemini 3.8 Flash, Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash (Team, 2026a) and many open-source models follow this recipe, and the field improves them mainly by making model size bigger and using more data (Cui et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). We think this recipe gets two things wrong. First, it assumes that the model must hear the audio directly (Cui et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b). In practice, most of the audio that questions depend on is speech (75.2% of the questions of LVOmniBench (Tao et al., 2026)), and speech is easily turned into text with time stamps. Teaching model to hear makes every new skill depend on costly joint training (Chowdhury et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025), and it weakens the reasoning and tool use that strong VLMs already have. Second, it assumes that one turn is enough. fixed sampling rate covers the whole video thinly, while the answer often sits in few seconds (Bai et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2026); in long video those seconds are easily missed, but this kind of model cannot go back (Chen et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Many works in video understanding have recognized this problem (Fan et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2025; Xing et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). The Qwen team runs Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash as agents in the Qwen Code harness and gains up to 10.3 points on long videos, and Video-Index (Song et al., 2026) finds that agent tools add about 20 points over fixed input. We agree: model should sleuth video for the evidence it needs rather than take in everything at once. The community should therefore rethink how omni models are built: omni models such as Qwen3-Omni, MiniCPM-o and video-SALMONN have the most to gain by moving from one turn to agentic understanding. Following this question, we propose SleuthVLM, which answers audio-visual questions with VLM that never hears the audio directly (Figure 2). The audio is transcribed once with word-level timestamps, and the VLM uses small set of tools to search the video and transcript. We specify only its accessible resources, brief agentic guide, and budget; the VLM decides where to look, how closely to inspect, and when to stop, using the transcript as an index to locate relevant moments in long videos. SleuthVLM establishes new state of the art (Figure 1), achieving an average accuracy of 75.0% across four omni benchmarks, 2.6 points above the strongest closed-source omni model, Gemini 3.8 Flash. It also leads every metric on the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard, reaching 77.8% accuracy, 6.8 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash. With Qwen3.8-27B, SleuthVLM outperforms every open-source omni model by 13.8 points. Our experiments reveal three findings: Searching outperforms passive observation. Agentic inference improves accuracy by up to 10.3 points, and our simple harness outperforms agents equipped with specialized tools. Agentic ability matters more than direct audio access. Even with access to audio, omni models in our harness perform below SleuthVLM with Opus 5.5, which relies on transcripts; omni models also need strong agentic capabilities. Small agentic models are highly competitive. An open 27B VLM running on single GPU 2 matches the performance of closed-source omni models. Taken together, SleuthVLM provides simple yet effective starting point for agentic omni video understanding.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Omnimodal Large Language Models. Omnimodal large language models aim to understand video, audio, and text within single model (Cui et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2025; Xie and Wu, 2024; Xu et al., 2025b). They typically extend vision-language model (VLM) with an audio encoder and train on large amounts of paired audio-visual data, enabling them to answer from sampled frames and audio in single pass. Open-source models following this approach include Qwen2.5-Omni (Xu et al., 2025a), Qwen3-Omni (Xu et al., 2025b), MiniCPM-o (Cui et al., 2026), the video-SALMONN series (Tang et al., 2025), LongCat-Flash-Omni (Team et al., 2025), and Nemotron-Nano-Omni (Deshmukh et al., 2026). Closed-source models such as Gemini, Qwen3.8Omni-Flash (Team, 2026a), and Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus (Team, 2026b) lead audio-visual benchmarks. Progress in this direction relies heavily on scaling data and models, while acquiring new capabilities requires costly multimodal training. Such training also costs part of the reasoning and tool-use abilities of strong VLMs, and single pass over fixed frame samples cannot revisit moments relevant to question. SleuthVLM instead uses VLM that accesses audio information through timestamped text and tools. Video Understanding Agent. Agents offer promising approach to understanding long and complex videos (Fan et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2025; Xing et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Early methods reason over clip captions or decompose questions into steps handled by specialized tools, while recent agents actively decide where to look. Audio-visual agents follow similar progression: OmniAgent (Tao et al., 2025) equips o3 with tools backed by separate models; OmniReasoner (Chen et al., 2026b) and OmniAgent-7B (Xing et al., 2026) train omni models to use tools; and the Qwen3.8-Omni report evaluates agents in the Qwen Code harness. TFO (Deria et al., 2026) provides frozen VLM with frames and speech transcript but answers in single pass. In contrast, SleuthVLM equips single VLM with general-purpose tools over video frames and timestamped transcript, allowing it to decide where to look, how closely to inspect, and when to stop. Concurrent methods also trail SleuthVLM: Omni-Decision (Ma et al., 2026) combines GPT-5.2 planner with Gemini-3.1-Pro perception, while sandboxed coding agents (Chen et al., 2026a) process videos using scripts and transcripts; both underperform Gemini-3.1-Pro in single pass. SleuthVLM exceeds Omni-Decision by 11.8 points on WorldSense and the best coding agent by 15.5 points on LVOmniBench (Section A).

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: SleuthVLM answers audio-visual questions using vision-language model (VLM) without direct access to audio. Instead, the audio is transcribed once per video with timestamps, and the VLM uses tools in sandbox to gather evidence until it can answer (Figure 2). 3 Figure 2 Overview of SleuthVLM. (a) Once per video, an ASR model transcribes the speech and forced aligner assigns timestamps to each word, preserving non-speech intervals as gaps. (b) VLM gathers evidence by calling tools over the muted video and transcript in sandbox; only omni reasoning models also have access to listen_audio. (c) The model answers once it has sufficient evidence, subject to fixed budgets. The illustrated trajectory is real example from Daily-Omni, answered correctly in 13 turns.

sections.title: 3.3 Agentic harness
sections.content: The harness consists of scope definition, which fixes what the model can access and do, and an operating guide, which suggests how to gather evidence; both are part of the system prompt and are the same on every benchmark. Scope definition. The files are the muted video, the question with its options, asr.txt and asr_words.tsv. The tools are bash, view (show images), watch (show short clip) and answer. Inside bash, vsheet renders contact sheet of time-stamped frames over [t0, t1], vframes extracts frames at chosen rate, optionally at native resolution, vcrop crops native-resolution frame, asr searches the transcript or lists word times and gaps, and standard tools such as grep and python3 are available. The rules keep the model inside its sandbox (relative paths, no network, no package or process commands, no audio extraction), and the budget = (Nturn, Nimg, Nclip, Tmax) limits the turns, viewed images, clips and time per question. Operating guide. The guide suggests sequence that usually works: read the question and the transcript, get an overview from one contact sheet, localize window from transcript hits, sheet cells and gaps, zoom in, check the detail asked about, and answer once the evidence decides the question. The model decides which steps question needs. Interaction. sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate on four omni video question-answering benchmarks, spanning videos from 30 seconds to 90 minutes: Daily-Omni (1,197 questions on 684 clips of 30 or 60 s), WorldSense (3,172 questions on 1,662 videos, averaging 2.4 min), OmniVideoBench (1,000 questions on 628 videos, averaging 6.4 min), and LVOmniBench (1,014 questions on 275 videos of 1090 min, averaging 34.6 min). We also evaluate on Video-MME-v2 (3,200 questions on 800 videos, averaging 10.4 min, with questions grouped in sets of four), which reports average accuracy and grouped nonlinear score across three difficulty levels. All questions are multiple choice. Compared methods. Table 1 compares SleuthVLM with closed-source and open-source omni models, as well as omni and VL + ASR agents. The agent baselines include OmniAgent, OmniReasoner, Qwen Code agents, and TFO. We use scores reported in the corresponding papers or technical reports; all closed-source results are from the Qwen3.8-Omni technical report. Implementation details. The reasoning model is Qwen3.8-27B, served with vLLM on H200/A100 GPUs; SleuthVLM (Opus 5.5) uses Claude Opus 5.5 instead and changes nothing else. All reasoning models run with high reasoning effort; the ablations in Section 4.3 and the results marked medium use Qwen3.8-27B with medium effort. The transcript is produced by Qwen3-ASR-1.7B and Qwen3ForcedAligner-0.6B, with gaps of γ = 3 s. On every benchmark, the budget is 50 turns, 30 images, 10 clips and 30 minutes per question. Omni reasoning models may also call listen_audio, up to 4 times on windows of at most 30 s. More details are in Section C.

sections.content: Table 1 compares SleuthVLM with frontier omni models and agents on the four benchmarks; SleuthVLM sets new state of the art both with closed-source and with an open reasoning model. Comparison with omni models. Without direct access to audio, SleuthVLM with Opus 5.5 achieves the highest average accuracy of 75.0%, outperforming all closed-source omni models. Its lead grows on longer-video benchmarks, reaching 4.7 points on OmniVideoBench and 4.8 points on LVOmniBench (Figure 3a), suggesting that agents benefit from revisiting evidence missed by fixed frame sampling. With an open 27B model, SleuthVLM outperforms the strongest open-source omni model by 13.8 points on average and 18.8 points on LVOmniBench; it also exceeds the similarly sized Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B by 16.8 points. Comparison with agents. sections.title: 5 Case Studies
sections.content: Figure 4 shows four trajectories with the decisive steps highlighted; Section walks through each of them turn by turn.

sections.title: 5.1 Answering from the timed transcript
sections.content: In Figure 4a, one search of the transcript lands at 20:37 of 38-minute show, and the model counts six people after viewing only the 20 seconds around it. In Figure 4b, the helicopter never appears on screen, but the transcript holds the speaker naming it: flybys with helicopter. Hear that?. The transcript gives the decisive clue, moment in (a) and the sound itself in (b), and the frames confirm it.

sections.title: 5.2 Hearing the music through a tool
sections.content: In Figure 4c, neither the transcript, single word, nor the frames tell how the music changes. One call to audio_caption on the first 30 returns fast opening that turns slow and gentle near 0:08, and the model checks it against the strumming in the frames.

sections.title: 5.3 Agentic ability: a VLM against an omni model
sections.content: In Figure 4d, Claude Opus 5.5, VLM, and Gemini 3.8 Flash, an omni model that may also see, answer the same question in the same harness: what was the host saying when viewer first commented, at 05:19 of an 83-minute stream? The key step is to bind the comment to the sentence spoken at that moment, same category of business. Opus 5.5 reads the frames and the transcript of the same window and binds them in five turns. Gemini 3.8 Flash finds the comment at 05:19 and the word business at 05:18.8, then rescans the whole video, listens to window that ends before the comment, and answers Money after 27 turns and 21 times the tokens. This is the agentic gap of Finding 2: trained on large amounts of audio-visual data to hear, the omni model loses the planning and evidence binding that VLM keeps.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We investigated whether omni video understanding requires direct audio access and introduced SleuthVLM, an agent harness that enables VLM to read word-timestamped transcript and autonomously search the video. SleuthVLM establishes new state of the art across four omni benchmarks and on Video-MME-v2. With Opus 5.5, it achieves an average accuracy of 75.0% across the four benchmarks, outperforming all closed-source omni model, and leads the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with 77.8%. With an open 27B VLM, it outperforms all open-source omni models by 13.8 points. Our results highlight three findings:1.Searching outperforms passive observation, 2. Agentic ability matters more than direct audio access, and 3. Small agentic models are highly competitive. SleuthVLM provides simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding.

sections.title: C Implementation details
sections.content: This section complements Section 4.1. Reasoning model and serving. Qwen3.8-27B runs in thinking mode with high reasoning effort (medium for the ablations and the results marked medium), sampled at temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 20, with at most 8192 generated tokens per turn (reasoning included) and up to four tool calls per turn. It is served with vLLM on one H200 GPU per shard, with sixteen questions in flight per GPU; finished question is replaced by the next one at once. Earlier reasoning stays in the history, so prompts only grow and the prefix cache is reused; when prompt exceeds 110k tokens, the oldest images are dropped from it. Claude Opus 5.5, Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash are called through APIs with the same harness, prompts and budget; time spent waiting on rate limits does not count towards Tmax. Commands. view shows up to four images per call, and contact sheet counts as one image; watch shows segment of at most 30 at 1 to 8 fps and at most 32 frames; vsheet tiles up to 64 time-stamped frames, vframes extracts up to 32 frames, and vcrop takes its box on 01000 scale of native-resolution frame. listen_audio returns mono 16 kHz clip of the original audio. Each command may run for 120 s, and at most 8000 characters of its output are kept in the conversation. Each question gets its own sandbox in memory, with muted copy of the video, and every command is logged. Transcription. Long recordings are cut at quiet points into pieces of at most 180 s, transcribed and aligned piecewise, and merged back on the videos time axis. When alignment fails, for example for language the aligner does not cover, the video is transcribed in 30 chunks and the transcript carries chunk-level times, with no word file. Transcribing the 3249 videos of the four benchmarks, about 302 hours of audio, takes about 113 minutes on single H200.

sections.title: G Sandbox rules and trajectory audit
sections.content: Rules. The sandbox of each question holds the muted video, question.md with the question and its options, and the two transcript files; none of them carries the answer. Commands run with the sandbox as working and home directory and minimal search path. Before command runs, guard checks it against fixed rules and refuses absolute paths to system directories, climbing out with .., network, package, process and system commands such as curl, wget, ssh, git, pip and sudo, the Python modules for network and process control, and extracting audio with ffmpeg. refused command is not run, and the model is told the reason. Every access is logged. The model acts only through four tools: view opens only image files inside the sandbox, watch plays only the sandbox video and answer ends the question, so any other file can be reached only through bash. Every bash command and its output are written to the result file, and every refused command is kept with its reason. Audit. We audit every trajectory and log of SleuthVLM (Qwen3.8-27B, medium) on the four benchmarks, 6,383 questions and 71,132 tool calls, including every command that builds path at run time. No command opens an annotation or result file, no output contains an answer, and every attempt to reach the network was refused: there is no answer leakage.
